questions.text: Consider a 2-dimensional array x with 10 rows and 4 columns, with each element storing a value equivalent to the product of row number and column number. The array is stored in row-major format. If the first element x[0][0] occupies the memory location with address 1000 and each element occupies only one memory location, which all locations (in decimal) will be holding a value of 10?
questions.solution:
Element (i, j) (0-based) holds (row number) [latex]\times[/latex] (column number) = (i + 1)(j + 1), and is stored at 1000 + 4i + j.

Value 10 = 5 [latex]\times[/latex] 2 or 10 [latex]\times[/latex] 1:
- row 5, column 2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] i = 4, j = 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 1000 + 16 + 1 = 1017
- row 10, column 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] i = 9, j = 0 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 1000 + 36 = 1036

Answer: 1017, 1036

Originally all Options are wrong. We have modified one option.

This is the juggling (cycle) method of rotating left by k. Each cycle starts at i and moves elements forward by k positions (mod n) until it returns to the start:
- outer loop while i [latex]\lt[/latex] min (cycles start at indices below the smallest visited)
- inner loop while j != (n + i [latex]-[/latex] k) mod n
- A[j] = A[(j + k) mod n], then the saved temp goes to position (n + i [latex]-[/latex] k) mod n, and i = i + 1

Answer: Option 4

options: [latex]i \lt \min ; \quad j !=(n+i-k) \bmod n ; \quad A[(j+k) \bmod n] \quad \text { temp; } \quad i+1 ;[/latex]

questions.text:
Let A be an array of 31 numbers consisting of sequence of 0's followed by a sequence of 1's.
The problem is to find the smallest index i that A[i] is 1 by probing the minimum numbers of
locations in A. The worst case number of probes performed by an optimal algorithm is
_____________.
questions.solution:
The array is sorted (0s then 1s), so binary search finds the first 1. 31 numbers give 32 possible answers (the first 1 can be at any position, or there are no 1s), which needs [latex]\log_2 32=5[/latex] probes.

Answer: 5

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

questions.text: The average number of key comparisons required for a successful search for sequential search on n items is
questions.solution:
If the key is equally likely to be at any of the n positions, finding it at position i takes i comparisons:
[latex]\frac{1+2+\cdots+n}{n}=\frac{n+1}{2}[/latex]

Answer: [latex]\frac{n+1}{2}[/latex]

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
